angle: Solo DTC brands get sold mid-market CDPs they don't need

posts.text:
# A solo DTC founder pays $50K a year for tools they already own

A bootstrapped direct-to-consumer brand pulling in a few million dollars a year is run by one full-time operator. No team, no ops department — one person making every infrastructure call.

That operator pays roughly $50K a year for an enterprise customer data platform (CDP) — a low single-digit percentage of revenue on one tool. The pitch for a CDP is unifying customer data across sources and computing traits like predicted lifetime value. Real capability. The question is whether a solo brand on Shopify needs a separate mid-market system to get it.

For most brands this size, the email platform and the storefront already cover the bulk of it: identity resolution, segments, automations, the events a CDP would forward anyway. The CDP becomes a second, parallel data layer that someone has to wire up, maintain, and justify — with no one on staff whose job that is.

None of this means CDPs are bad. It means tools get sold at a tier above the buyer. If you're a lean operator, the useful audit isn't "is the bill too high" — it's "what does this do that my email + storefront don't, and is any of it actually wired up and driving revenue?" If you can't answer that in a sentence, you're paying enterprise prices for a capability you already own.

A solo-run DTC brand doing a few million a year was paying ~$50K/yr for an enterprise CDP — low-single-digit % of revenue on one tool its email + storefront already largely covered. The useful question isn't 'is the bill high' but 'what does this do that my existing stack doesn't?'
